description: We are a team of enthusiastic students from the National University of Singapore, passionate about bridging the gap between astrophysics and artificial intelligence. We are excited to leverage upon our analytical skills, to uncover variables and environment for space exploration!
summary: What if the best place to prepare for Mars is somewhere on Earth we haven't discovered yet? Earth holds countless environments that resemble landscapes of Mars, yet many potential analog sites remain unexplored. Finding them manually is time-consuming, geographically limited, and difficult to scale. We developed an end-to-end planetary analog discovery pipeline that transforms Earth into a searchable laboratory for Mars exploration. Starting with scientifically documented Mars analog sites, our system identifies meaningful environmental and geological signatures using open Earth observation datasets. We integrate elevation, terrain roughness, temperature, humidity, vegetation, lithology, and mineral proxies to characterize what makes these locations scientifically relevant. Through a two-stage discovery process, we first eliminate unsuitable regions using large-scale geospatial filtering, then rank promising candidates through multidimensional similarity analysis. Our goal goes beyond rediscovering known analogs: we aim to uncover overlooked terrestrial environments that could advance planetary science. By systematically identifying and characterizing potential Mars analogs, our solution could help researchers prioritize field investigations, test exploration technologies, and better prepare humanity for future missions to Mars.
details:
Introduction

Scientists have long used Earth's extreme environments to simulate geological and environmental conditions on Mars. However, discovering suitable analog locations remains a challenging process, often dependent on previously studied sites and manual geographical investigation. As such, we developed a planetary analog discovery system that searches Earth's surface for environments with characteristics similar to scientifically established Mars analogs. By combining NASA Earth observation datasets, satellite imagery, geological information, and geospatial similarity analysis, our system identifies and ranks candidate locations that could support future planetary research and mission preparation.

Methodology

Our approach consists of three main phases.

Phase 1: Building Scientifically Grounded Reference Profiles

We identified the relevant planetary processes and environmental characteristics studied in existing research literature for terrestrial Mars analog environments such as McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica, Mauna Loa in Hawaii, Haughton Impact Crater in Canada, and Askja Caldera in Iceland. 

To construct measurable environmental profiles, we integrate multiple datasets:

  • Copernicus DEM GLO-30: Elevation, slope, terrain relief, and terrain ruggedness.
  • Sentinel-2 Level-2A: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), vegetation coverage, and bare-ground fraction.
  • Landsat Collection 2 Level-2: Alternative optical satellite observations and NDVI.
  • NASA MODIS MOD11A1: Summer maximum and winter minimum land-surface temperatures.
  • NASA MODIS MOD10A1: Snow-cover persistence.
  • NASA POWER: Air temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, and number of days above freezing.
  • Global Lithological Map (GLiM): Dominant regional rock types and lithological classifications.
  • Earth Impact Database: Distance to known terrestrial impact structures.
  • NASA EMIT L2B Mineralogy: Mineral-data discovery, with potential future extraction of clay, sulfate, and iron-mineral fractions.

NASA's open Earth observation datasets form the foundation of our discovery pipeline. We use NASA MODIS satellite data to analyze land-surface temperature extremes and snow-cover persistence, while NASA POWER provides climate measurements such as precipitation, humidity, and air temperature. These datasets allow our system to capture different environmental similarity rather than relying solely on satellite imagery. For each reference location, we analyze a 1 km × 1 km geographical window, extracting numerical features such as elevation, roughness, vegetation scarcity, temperature extremes, precipitation, lithology.

Phase 2: Searching Earth Through Hierarchical Geospatial Filtering

A major challenge is the enormous computational cost of analyzing the entire planet at high spatial resolution. To overcome this, we developed a coarse-to-fine global search architecture using HEALPix  At the coarse level, Earth is divided into 196,608 approximately 50 km-scale regions. Our prefilter examines regional environmental characteristics and eliminates areas whose available measurements are incompatible with the characteristics of known analog locations.Rather than arbitrarily removing regions, our algorithm uses a recall-preserving strategy: a region is rejected only when its observed feature range cannot overlap the acceptable range of a reference site.Regions with missing measurements remain eligible for further evaluation rather than being incorrectly classified as unsuitable. This approach substantially reduces unnecessary fine-resolution processing while prioritizing the retention of potentially valuable candidates.

Phase 3: Fine-Resolution Similarity Search and Ranking

Regions surviving the global prefilter are expanded into finer HEALPix cells, where approximately 1 km geographical windows are evaluated. We extract environmental features using the same methods applied to our reference sites, ensuring consistent comparisons. We compare candidate locations with known Mars analog sites using normalized Euclidean distance. Features are scaled using the interquartile range (IQR) to ensure that variables such as elevation, temperature, and humidity contribute fairly to the comparison. We then convert the distance into a similarity score between 0 and 1, where a higher score indicates a closer match. This allows us to rank potential Mars analog locations based on their environmental similarities. The system also records which features contributed to each comparison, the number of comparable measurements, and whether the dominant lithology matches. Rather than simply returning a list of coordinates, our approach provides evidence to help researchers understand why a location may be scientifically relevant.

Technologies and Tools

Our system is implemented primarily in Python and React.

  • NumPy, Pandas, and SciPy: Numerical processing, feature extraction, environmental statistics, and similarity calculations.
  • Rasterio and GDAL: Geospatial raster access, reprojection, resampling, and digital elevation model processing.
  • GeoPandas, Shapely, and PyProj: Geographical geometry processing, coordinate transformations, and geological spatial analysis.
  • Healpy / HEALPix: Hierarchical global spatial indexing and efficient coarse-to-fine geographical search.
  • Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API: Access to Copernicus DEM, Sentinel-2, Landsat, and MODIS satellite products.
  • NASA POWER API: Historical meteorological and climatological observations.
  • Google Earth Engine: Alternative processing pathway for MODIS land-surface temperature and snow-cover products.
  • NASA Earthdata / Earthaccess: Discovery of EMIT mineralogy observations.
  • Git and GitHub: Collaborative software development and version control.

We made use of Google Cloud Virtual Machine for computation.

Project Novelty

Firstly, we search beyond familiar locations. Existing analog sites provide scientific guidance, but our system is designed to discover potentially overlooked regions that may offer equally valuable research opportunities. Moreover, we also ensured that the proposed candidate sites were backed by the same research process being studied at current analogs to provide similar conditions for experiments. Secondly, we go beyond visual similarity. Our approach combines topography, climate, vegetation, geological context, and seasonal surface conditions. This allows us to distinguish locations that merely look similar from those that share measurable environmental characteristics. Lastly, in order to make search scaleable, we combined hierarchical HEALPix indexing with conservative spatial prefiltering and avoided expensive high-resolution analysis across every location on Earth.

Our objective is not simply to identify places resembling Mars, but to identify environments that may help scientists investigate specific Martian geological processes, surface conditions, and exploration challenges.

Scientific Considerations

We carefully considered the limitations of planetary analog research.No terrestrial location can perfectly reproduce Mars. Differences in gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, and planetary history mean that environmental resemblance must be interpreted carefully. Moreover, a location with similar temperatures and surface conditions may still possess very different geology. Likewise, a volcanic landscape may provide a meaningful geological analogy without reproducing Martian atmospheric conditions. We therefore distinguish between different dimensions of similarity and retain information about missing measurements, dataset coverage, and geological differences. Additionally, we also account for differences in spatial resolution. High-resolution elevation and optical data support detailed local analysis, while coarser climate products provide broader environmental context.This helps prevent our system from presenting satellite-derived proxies as direct evidence of identical planetary processes.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our project has the potential to improve how scientists identify and prioritize terrestrial analog environments. For planetary scientists, it provides a systematic method for identifying candidate locations that may help investigate Martian geological and environmental processes. For mission engineers, it could support the selection of terrestrial test environments for robotic systems, navigation technologies, and exploration instruments.For research teams, it reduces the initial search space and provides a reproducible, data-driven foundation for deciding which locations deserve closer investigation. For the broader scientific community, it demonstrates how openly accessible Earth observation data can be integrated into a scalable tool for planetary exploration research. While candidate locations still require expert evaluation and field validation, our system can make the earliest stages of analog discovery more efficient and evidence-driven.

Future works

First, expanding feature coverage and geographical sampling. Our current approach evaluates a limited sample of candidate patches using selected environmental and geological features. Future development could incorporate additional datasets, such as soil composition, mineralogy, subsurface ice, and atmospheric conditions, while expanding the search to cover more patches at finer resolutions. This would enable a more comprehensive assessment of potential analog sites and reduce the risk of overlooking promising locations. Second, enabling real-time planetary analog discovery. Our current deployment relies on precomputed data and similarity rankings. Future iterations could introduce on-demand inference, allowing researchers to select or scan a region on Mars and automatically identify corresponding terrestrial analogs based on its geological and environmental characteristics. This would transform our system from a static discovery tool into an interactive platform connecting Martian environments with relevant locations on Earth.

Conclusion

Our project demonstrates how satellite observations, geospatial analysis, and similarity-based search can transform the way we discover terrestrial Mars analogs. By moving beyond well-known research sites and visual resemblance, we provide a systematic approach to identifying overlooked environments that could support planetary science and future exploration missions. We envision a future where Earth becomes a searchable planetary laboratory, helping researchers discover new test sites, investigate Martian processes, and prepare exploration technologies more efficiently. Ultimately, we hope to bridge the gap between studying Mars from afar and preparing for its exploration here on Earth. Because the next breakthrough in Mars exploration might not begin on Mars, but somewhere on Earth we have yet to discover.
